newsitem.title: GERMANY: Steffi Graf's father heads home from prison.
newsitem.headline: Steffi Graf's father heads home from prison.

text.p: Tennis star Steffi Graf's father paid five million marks ($3.3 million) in bail and headed home from prison on Friday after being held in investigative custody for the last 15 months.
A German court trying him on tax evasion charges ruled he no longer needed to remain in custody after an objection by prosecutors was rejected by a higher court later in the day.

Peter Graf slipped through the courtroom back door, shook the hands of his lawyers and friends, and left in a brown car -- the kind he used to sell before becoming a regular on the tennis VIP circuit.

"I want to be at home," he told journalists. When asked if he had telephoned his daughter Steffi who is playing in a tournament in Philadelphia, Graf shook his head. He was not allowed to say any more as the case is still continuing.

The Mannheim court said Graf, 58, would have to report to police twice a week and receive pyschotherapy. His mental health during his time in custody has been the subject of German newspaper speculation.
Graf has always been an important figure in the life of his millionaire daughter. They were virtually inseparable until Graf was arrested in August last year after tax officials raided their homes.
Although Steffi, 27, has performed remarkably well in the last 15 months, she has broken down several times in public when asked about the pressure of the tax affair.
Family financial adviser Joachim Eckardt was also released on bail after paying 300,000 marks and handing in his passport.
Graf's lawyer Franz Salditt told reporters: "We will celebrate together in a quieter place."
Graf could be taken back into custody if the Karlsruhe court upholds other objections from the prosecution, but Salditt said he did not know whether this would happen.
Graf is accused of evading 19 million marks ($13 million) of tax on his daughter's earnings between 1989 and 1993.
Steffi says she knew little about her financial affairs, entrusting them to her father from the start of a career which has taken her to the number one spot in women's tennis.

The Mannheim court ruled Graf was unlikely to skip bail because of his strong ties to Germany and his commitment to holding on to Steffi's earnings. It said he wouldn't want to jeopardise this by breaking his bail conditions.
"He also knows what the personal and professional results would be for his daughter if he was to flee," the ruling said.
After handing over a banker's draft and his passport, he left the courtroom, mobbed by cameramen and reporters.
